text: Best Buy Co., Inc. was incorporated in Minnesota in 1966 and operates in the United States, Canada, and Mexico, striving to enrich consumers' lives through technology by solving technology problems and addressing key human needs in areas such as entertainment, productivity, communication, food preparation, security, and health and wellness. The company has two reportable segments: Domestic and International. The Domestic segment includes operations across all U.S. states, districts, and territories under brands such as Best Buy, bestbuy.com, Best Buy Direct, Best Buy Express, Best Buy Mobile, Geek Squad, GreatCall, Magnolia, and Pacific Kitchen and Home. The International segment includes operations in Canada and Mexico under the brands Best Buy, Best Buy Express, Best Buy Mobile, Geek Squad, and the domain names bestbuy.ca and bestbuy.com.mx. On March 1, 2018, Best Buy announced its intent to close all 257 of its remaining Best Buy Mobile stand-alone stores in the U.S., which were fully closed during the second quarter of fiscal 2019. On October 1, 2018, the company acquired all outstanding shares of GreatCall, Inc., a leading connected health services provider for aging consumers offering easy-to-use mobile products and connected devices. The Domestic and International segments operate a multi-channel platform enabling customers to engage with the company online, in stores, or in their homes. The Domestic segment centrally manages merchandise development, pricing, procurement, supply chain, online and mobile operations, marketing, and labor deployment, with support functions like human resources and finance managed from corporate headquarters. Field operations support retail, services, and in-home teams from corporate and regional locations, and store procedures for inventory, asset protection, transactions, customer relations, sales, staff training, and merchandise display are largely standardized with flexibility for local market conditions. The International segment operates similarly to the Domestic segment. Revenue is generated through six categories: Computing and Mobile Phones, Consumer Electronics, Appliances, Entertainment, Services, and Other. Key components include computing and peripherals, e-readers, mobile phones (including carrier commissions), networking, tablets, wearables, digital imaging, health and fitness, home theater, portable audio, smart home, major and small appliances, drones, gaming hardware and software, movies, music, toys, virtual reality, consultation, delivery, design, installation, memberships, protection plans, repair, set-up, technical support, and GreatCall offerings, as well as beverages, snacks, sundries, baby products, luggage, and sporting goods in the International segment. Customers purchasing online can choose to pick up items at U.S. Best Buy stores or have them delivered from distribution centers or retail stores, with most merchandise shipped directly from manufacturers to distribution centers, and some shipped directly to stores to meet release dates. The Canada and Mexico distribution models mirror the Domestic model. In fiscal 2019, the company’s 20 largest suppliers accounted for approximately 64% of merchandise purchased, with five suppliers—Apple, Samsung, Hewlett-Packard, Sony, and LG—accounting for about 51% of total purchases. The company does not have long-term written contracts with vendors and instead manages inventory through continuous monitoring of consumer demand, adjustment of inventory receipt levels and pricing, vendor agreements for markdown reimbursements and return privileges, and a global sourcing operation that designs, develops, tests, and contracts the manufacture of exclusive brand products. As of the end of fiscal 2019, Best Buy had 1,187 large-format and 51 small-format stores across its Domestic and International segments, with all U.S. and large-format Canadian stores capable of shipping from store locations and allowing online orders to be picked up in any store. Beginning in 2013, the company opened vendor store-within-a-store concepts to strengthen vendor partnerships and improve the customer experience. For fiscal 2020 and beyond, Best Buy plans to optimize store space, renegotiate leases, and selectively open or close locations. The company owns or has rights to use valuable intellectual property, including trademarks and service marks such as Best Buy, Best Buy Express, Best Buy Mobile, Dynex, Geek Squad, GreatCall, Insignia, Jitterbug, Lively, Magnolia, Modal, My Best Buy, Pacific Sales, Pacific Kitchen and Home, Platinum, Rocketfish, 5Star, and its Yellow Tag logo, and holds domestic and international trademark and service mark registrations as well as patents for many of its inventions. The company’s business is seasonal, with a significant portion of revenue and earnings generated in the fiscal fourth quarter, which includes the major holiday shopping season in the U.S., Canada, and Mexico. Operations are funded through available cash, cash equivalents, short-term investments, operating cash flows, and revolving credit facilities, with working capital needs increasing in the months leading up to the holiday season due to inventory purchases. Competitors include multi-channel retailers, e-commerce businesses, technology service providers, traditional retailers, vendors, and mobile network carriers. Best Buy believes its ability to serve customers online, in stores, and in their homes, and to connect technology solutions with customer needs, provides key competitive advantages. Some competitors have lower operating costs and focus on price, but a June 2018 Supreme Court decision in South Dakota v. Wayfair allowed states to require online-only retailers to collect and remit sales taxes, eroding the price advantage of some competitors. Best Buy monitors competitor pricing and maintains price-matching policies to match prices offered by certain retail stores and online operators, supported by efficient operations and global vendor partnerships. Key competitive advantages include dedicated and knowledgeable employees, integrated online, retail, and in-home assets, a broad and curated product assortment, strong vendor partnerships, service offerings that solve real customer needs, unique store formats for showcasing technology, and a robust supply chain. The company is committed to values-driven leadership and sustainable development, expanding employee benefits to include enhanced mental health coverage, backup childcare, caregiver leave, and paid time off for part-time employees, and reinforcing its commitment to diversity and inclusion by signing the CEO Action for Diversity & Inclusion Pledge and the Parity Pledge.

Best Buy offers competitive pricing to consumers, matching or undercutting prices from certain retail stores and online operators. To maintain this, the company focuses on efficient operations and leverages economies of scale through global vendor partnerships. Key elements of its competitive advantage include dedicated and knowledgeable employees, integrated online, retail, and in-home services, a broad and curated product selection, strong vendor relationships, service offerings that address real customer needs, unique store formats for showcasing technology, and a robust supply chain. The company is committed to values-driven leadership and sustainable development, applying corporate responsibility to all stakeholders, including customers, employees, vendors, shareholders, communities, and the environment. Employee benefits have been expanded to include enhanced mental health coverage, backup childcare, caregiver leave, and paid time off for part-time workers. Best Buy has signed the CEO Action for Diversity & Inclusion Pledge and the Parity Pledge to reinforce its commitment to diversity and inclusion. To support teens from underserved communities, the company operates 25 Best Buy Teen Tech Centers, which provide technology exposure, professional skill development, and mentorship from Best Buy employees, with a plan to reach 60 centers over the next few years. The company has achieved a significant reduction in carbon emissions, reaching a 60% decrease by 2020 (based on a 2009 baseline) through operational improvements and renewable energy sourcing. It also promotes sustainability by offering ENERGY STAR® certified products to help customers save on utility bills and collected over 180 million pounds of consumer electronics and appliances for recycling in fiscal 2019. At the end of fiscal 2019, Best Buy employed nearly 125,000 full-time, part-time, and seasonal employees across the U.S., Canada, and Mexico, offering a range of company-paid benefits that are competitive locally and in aggregate within the industry. Key risks include strong competition from multi-channel retailers, e-commerce businesses, technology service providers, traditional retailers, vendors, and mobile network carriers, which directly affect revenue and profitability due to price transparency and real-time price comparisons. The retail sector is shifting toward online and mobile-driven sales, with customers demanding faster, guaranteed delivery times and low or free shipping, putting pressure on Best Buy’s delivery capabilities and potentially impacting margins. The company’s strategy to expand into new products, services, and technologies introduces financial, regulatory, and operational risks, including limited experience in new markets, potential service disruptions, and exposure to privacy and information security regulations such as the Health Insurance Portability and Accountability Act (HIPAA). Acquiring GreatCall in fiscal 2019, which provides emergency concierge and monitoring services, exposes the company to liability risks related to service failures, data security, and system interruptions. Offering a wide range of services—such as installation, repair, technical support, and health and safety monitoring—increases risks including higher labor costs, service errors, warranty failures, expanded liability due to employee access to customer devices, third-party involvement in installations, and non-compliance with laws and regulations. Best Buy sources products from a wide range of domestic and international vendors; in fiscal 2019, its 20 largest suppliers accounted for approximately 64% of merchandise purchased (70% in fiscal 2018), with five suppliers—Apple, Samsung, Hewlett-Packard, Sony, and LG—accounting for about 51% of total purchases (56% in fiscal 2018). The company generally does not have long-term contracts with vendors and depends on securing favorable terms for pricing, promotions, payment terms, product allocations, promotional experiences, and returns. Vendors may leverage their financial strength, brand power, or retail presence to disadvantage Best Buy, especially when purchases represent a small portion of their revenue or when competition is low. The company also relies on a small number of mobile carriers to offer mobile devices with carrier connections; changes in carrier contracts, upgrade terms, fees, or service levels could reduce new customer contracts and impact revenue. Employee retention and recruitment are critical, as turnover in retail, service, and field positions can impair operations and growth. Market increases in compensation, especially for field employees, could negatively affect profitability. The company faces significant compliance and legal risks, including conflicting regulations, environmental laws, product safety requirements, data privacy laws such as the California Consumer Privacy Act (CCPA), which went into effect on January 1, 2020 and may require changes to data practices and incur additional costs, as well as potential amendments to the law. Other risks include evolving financial, labor, healthcare, and corporate governance regulations, restrictive trade policies, higher tariffs, tax law changes, and litigation trends involving consumers, shareholders, and labor. Regulatory scrutiny in the retail sector increases compliance costs and risks of fines. Defending against lawsuits is costly and diverts management attention. Macroeconomic factors such as GDP growth, consumer confidence, inflation, interest rates, employment, oil prices, and foreign exchange rates influence consumer spending, brand choices, device upgrades, and demand for services. Failure to manage costs effectively—despite fixed or long-term cost elements—could harm profitability and limit funding for growth initiatives. The company relies heavily on its information technology systems for core operations, including demand forecasting, purchasing, supply chain, point-of-sale, service fulfillment, staffing, financial management, and data security. These systems are vulnerable to outages, cyberattacks, viruses, denial-of-service attacks, natural disasters, and human error, and any failure could disrupt operations, increase costs, and result in lost revenue. The company also uses complex IT platforms to operate its websites and mobile applications, and disruptions to these platforms could impact service delivery.

Our business is heavily reliant on information technology systems to manage key operations, including demand forecasting, purchasing, supply chain management, point-of-sale processing, services fulfillment, staff planning, financial management, reporting, forecasting, and the safeguarding of sensitive data. These systems, along with those of our technology vendors and partners, are vulnerable to failures from power outages, computer or telecommunications failures, viruses, worms, malicious software, denial-of-service attacks, security breaches, catastrophic events like fires, tornadoes, earthquakes, or hurricanes, and employee errors. Any failure or interruption could significantly disrupt operations, increase costs, reduce revenues, and threaten our ability to remain in business. We also operate complex platforms for our websites and mobile applications; if we fail to secure them or maintain and upgrade our hardware, software, network, and infrastructure, disruptions may occur due to unforeseen traffic, malicious attacks, technical issues, or events beyond our control—such as natural disasters or data loss—leading to missed customer orders, lost revenue, and reputational harm. Breaches of customer, employee, vendor, or company data—whether from cyber-attacks, control lapses, or employee misconduct—could result in substantial costs, litigation, and reputational damage. We collect and store sensitive customer data, including payment card information, and share confidential data with third parties; vulnerabilities in products we sell or service, such as on customer-owned devices, may lead to data compromises. Increasing costs for information security, compliance, fraud, and insurance, along with new regulations like the General Data Protection Regulation and CCPA, require additional resources and increase breach risks. Any data compromise could raise protection costs and legal exposure. We may enter into new ventures, partnerships, or acquisitions, which carry significant risks, including failure to integrate operations, retain key personnel, forecast performance, generate synergies, or maintain financial controls, and could impair liquidity, profitability, or divert management attention. A large portion of our revenue and earnings comes from the fourth fiscal quarter, which includes the majority of the U.S., Canadian, and Mexican holiday shopping season, making it difficult to forecast due to unpredictable factors like competitive activity, consumer demand, economic shifts, cyber-attacks, or system failures. The industry is rapidly evolving due to technological innovation, product life cycle changes, and shifting consumer preferences, and failure to adapt could result in offering outdated products, excess inventory, supply shortages, delayed responses to trends, or brand damage. Our promotional financing and credit card programs—used by approximately 25% of fiscal 2019 revenue—generate profit-sharing income and are subject to transaction volume, financing terms, bad debt rates, interest rates, regulatory changes, and competition; adverse changes could reduce customer access to financing and lower our earnings. Our supply chain, critical due to trends like ship-from-store and fast delivery, depends on vendors delivering products on time and in the right quantities, and risks include delivery interruptions, third-party failures, system disruptions, capacity limits, transportation sector consolidation, labor strikes, product damage, and rising transportation costs. Inefficient supply chain operations or disruptions could harm revenue and profitability, especially in small parcel deliveries where few carriers meet our needs. Catastrophic events such as natural disasters, diseases, fires, or terrorism could disrupt operations, damage property, disable supply chains, and affect IT systems, leading to lost revenue and profitability. Declines in brand perception—due to poor service, pricing, delivery failures, or negative public comments—can reduce revenues, customer loyalty, gift card sales, employee retention, and vendor relationships. Product safety and quality failures may lead to legal risks, regulatory enforcement, and product recalls, especially if replacement products are unavailable, negatively impacting revenue and profitability. Changes in labor laws—such as unionization, independent contractor regulations, or minimum wage and leave requirements—could increase payroll costs and affect service delivery; even though as of February 2, 2019, no U.S. operations had unionized employees, future organizing could increase costs and impact operations. Poor management of our real estate portfolio—such as failing to secure suitable store locations or misjudging store layouts, demand, or lease terms—could impair competitiveness and profitability, with consequences like store closures, costly remodels, or excessive lease expenses. Exiting leased properties may incur significant costs due to lease terms, market conditions, or lack of sub-lease tenants, and we remain liable for taxes, insurance, and common area maintenance on vacant properties. Sub-lease defaults also expose us to liability. Constraints in capital markets or tighter vendor credit terms could reduce our liquidity, forcing operational curtailments or limiting business opportunities. Our primary liquidity sources are operating cash flow, cash reserves, investments, credit facilities, debt arrangements, and trade payables; reduced vendor payment terms or tighter credit limits could strain liquidity. If we fail to secure sufficient financing, our borrowing costs and access to capital could increase, and our ability to meet obligations may be threatened. Downgrades in our credit ratings could reduce market access, raise borrowing costs, and negatively affect vendor and lease terms, as ratings are subject to change due to external factors like new methodologies. We rely on third-party vendors for IT, web hosting, HR, customer loyalty, financing, gift cards, warranty, delivery, support, transportation, and insurance; any material disruption in these relationships or services could impact revenues, costs, and operations, especially during peak periods. Our exclusive brand products—such as Dynex, Insignia, Modal, Platinum, and Rocketfish—are manufactured in southeast Asia, exposing us to risks including greater warranty liability, limited recourse to manufacturers in foreign jurisdictions, and potential regulatory or product liability claims, including recalls, which could materially affect our operating results.

Sales of the company’s exclusive brand products—Dynex, Insignia, Modal, Platinum, and Rocketfish—represent a significant part of its revenue and profitability. These products are primarily manufactured by contract manufacturers located in southeast Asia, which introduces several risks that could materially affect operating results. These risks include greater consumer responsibility for warranty claims due to product defects, limited recourse to manufacturers in foreign jurisdictions, potential regulatory compliance and product liability claims—some of which may require recalls—disruptions in manufacturing or logistics from inconsistent order patterns, inability to form long-term relationships with manufacturers, or unforeseen natural disasters, difficulty in finding manufacturers that meet internal quality and safety standards, increased risk of inventory obsolescence due to the absence of return-to-vendor rights, exposure to changing labor and environmental laws in foreign countries, potential intellectual property infringement claims or failure to pay royalties, disruptions from trade disputes or excessive tariffs that may prevent timely sourcing of alternatives, inability to secure or protect patents and intellectual property rights, and increased costs and reputational harm from regulations requiring disclosure of the origin of “conflict minerals” in the supply chain. Maintaining consistent quality, availability, and competitive pricing of these products is essential for customer loyalty, revenue generation, and profitability; failure to do so could significantly reduce demand and profits. The company is also exposed to risks related to vendors sourcing products outside the U.S., including political or economic instability, trade restrictions, tariffs, quality or safety issues, work stoppages, port delays, foreign currency fluctuations, transportation constraints, inflation, civil unrest, natural disasters, pandemics, and vendor underinvestment in facilities or changes in pricing or promotional policies. These factors could have a material adverse impact on financial results. The company operates retail locations in Canada and Mexico, with most exclusive brand products manufactured in southeast Asia, and has wholly owned legal entities in Barbados, Bermuda, China, Hong Kong, Luxembourg, Mauritius, Turks and Caicos, and the U.K. During fiscal 2019, the International segment generated 8% of total revenue. Risks applicable to the domestic operations also apply internationally, with additional risks including political events like war or terrorism, economic conditions such as monetary policies and foreign exchange risk, changes in international trade rules or ownership regulations, cultural differences, variations in employee relations practices, difficulties in enforcing intellectual property rights, and challenges in managing remote operations. Revenue and operating profit growth depend on global demand for the company’s products and services, and are affected by worldwide economic and business conditions. If financial results fail to meet guidance or market expectations, or if guidance is reduced, the market price of the company’s common stock may decline. Kamy Scarlett was appointed Chief Human Resources Officer at Best Buy in June 2017 and became President, U.S. Retail Stores in January 2019. In this role, she oversees talent development and the health and well-being of the nearly 125,000 Best Buy employees worldwide, as well as the execution and operation of all domestic Best Buy store locations. She joined Best Buy in 2014 and has held various retail operations, marketing, and human resources leadership positions since beginning her career in retail over 30 years ago. Most recently, she served as senior vice president of retail and chief human resources officer for Best Buy Canada from 2014 to May 2017, where she was responsible for sales and profits in more than 180 stores and implemented human resources and talent management strategies. Prior to joining Best Buy, she was chief operating officer at Grafton-Fraser Inc. from 2012 to 2014, a leading Canadian retailer of men’s apparel. She also held leadership roles at Loblaw Cos., Hudson’s Bay Co., and Dylex Inc. Ms. Scarlett serves on the boards of directors of Greater MSP and The Best Buy Foundation. R. Michael (Mike) Mohan has served as Chief Operating Officer, Best Buy U.S. since September 2018. His responsibilities include oversight of all customer channels for Best Buy’s domestic business, including retail, ecommerce, customer experience, services, home, and Best Buy Direct, as well as leadership in category management, merchandising, marketing, supply chain, and real estate for the core U.S. business. Before this role, he was senior executive vice president and chief merchandising and marketing officer from 2017 to September 2018; chief merchandising officer from 2014 to 2017; president, home from 2013 to 2014; senior vice president, general manager - home business group from 2011 to 2013; senior vice president, home theatre from 2008 to 2011; and vice president, home entertainment from 2006 to 2008. Prior to joining Best Buy in 2004 as vice president, digital imaging, he was vice president and general merchandising manager for Good Guys, an audio/video specialty retailer in the western U.S. He also worked at Future Shop in Canada from 1988 to 1997, prior to Best Buy’s acquisition of the company, in various merchandising roles. Mr. Mohan serves on the board of directors of Bloomin’ Brands, a hospitality industry company that owns several American casual dining restaurant chains, and as a national trustee for the Boys & Girls Clubs of America. Keith J. Nelsen has served as General Counsel and Secretary since 2011, managing the enterprise legal function and acting as Secretary to the Board of Directors. Previously, he served as chief risk officer from 2012 to 2013. He was appointed executive vice president, general counsel in May 2011 and secretary in June 2011, having served as senior vice president, commercial and international general counsel from 2008 until his current appointment. Mr. Nelsen joined Best Buy in 2006 as vice president, operations and international general counsel. Prior to that, he worked at Danka Business Systems PLC from 1997 to 2006, holding roles including chief administration officer and general counsel, and at NordicTrack, Inc. from 1995 to 1997 as vice president, legal. He began his career in 1989 as a practicing attorney with Best and Flanagan, LLP, a law firm in Minneapolis, Minnesota. Mr. Nelsen is a member of the board of directors of NuShoe, Inc., a privately held shoe repair facility in San Diego, California. Brian Tilzer has served as Chief Digital and Technology Officer since May 2018, responsible for all aspects of information technology and digital at Best Buy to create a seamless and superior multichannel customer experience in support of the company’s Best Buy 2020 growth strategy. With over 25 years of experience in strategic business development, operations, and information technology, Mr. Tilzer has deep expertise in defining and delivering technology for superior customer experiences in multichannel environments. Prior to joining Best Buy, he was chief digital officer at CVS Health, the largest pharmacy healthcare provider in the U.S. He also served as senior vice president of e-commerce for Staples and senior vice president of strategy and business development for Linens ’n Things.
